```{r}
#| label: options
#| include: false
options(housepi.footer.warranty = TRUE)
options(housepi.footer.sample = TRUE)
```

Here we show how to measure the performance of inference at known parameter values, and how it changes with the sample size.
A single replicate can miss the truth by chance, while many of them show whether it misses systematically.
Performance checks simulate many studies at the same parameter values, fit each one back with the same model, and compare the estimates against the truth.
This is a simulation study in the sense of @morris_using_2019.
Repeated sampling at one value measures the frequentist properties of the posterior, such as its bias and the coverage of its credible intervals.
[Simulation-based calibration](simulation_calibration_checks.html) instead draws a new truth for every replicate, and checks the posterior as a whole.

We use the same final-size example presented in [Get started](housepi.html):

```{r}
#| label: inference-setup
# repeat inference as in 'Get Started'
library(housepi)
set_housepi_theme(colour_strips = TRUE)
set_housepi_summary(cri_level = 0.95)
set.seed(42)

hh_model <- flu_1918_frederick |>
  new_housepi_model("final-size") |>
  add_parameter(import = "template")

# store posterior draws
hh_fit <- hh_model |>
  run_inference(threads = 2)

hh_fit
```

The fit above estimates the model parameters.
We check whether a dataset similar to the target one, simulated at the estimated parameters, would let inference recover them.

# Performance at the estimates

Passing the fit as `truth` simulates every study at its point estimates.
To test values of your own choosing, pass one value per parameter, as in `c(alpha = 0.15, beta = 0.2, gamma = 1)`.

Each study is generated on households drawn with replacement from the attached data by `sample_house_structure()`, so it keeps the original household-size distribution, while the model draws who gets infected.
The results then describe a population of households shaped like those of Frederick.
Besides the observed number of households, we ask what a quarter, half and twice as many would give:

```{r}
#| label: house-counts
# number of households in target data
n_houses <- length(unique(flu_1918_frederick$hh_id))
# household sample sizes for power analysis
houses <- round(n_houses * c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2))
houses
```

A check costs one fit per replicate and household sample size, and larger studies take longer to fit.
We can run different replicates at each sample size using `check_performance()`:

```{r}
#| label: sweep
performance <- hh_model |>
  check_performance(hh_fit, nrep = 15, houses = houses, threads = 2)
performance

# overview of the checks per sample size, averaged over replicates
performance$overview
```

```{r}
#| label: sweep-cost
#| include: false
sweep_minutes <- with(performance$overview, sum(nrep * mean_inference_secs)) / 60
```

Fits slow down as the study grows, which sets the budget of a longer check.
Here the `r sum(performance$overview$nrep)` fits took `r round(sweep_minutes, 1)` min on one thread, from `r round(min(performance$overview$mean_inference_secs), 1)` s each at `r min(houses)` households to `r round(max(performance$overview$mean_inference_secs), 1)` s at `r max(houses)`.

A fit whose draws do not pass the convergence diagnostics is counted as flagged.
Here the diagnostics flagged `r sum(performance$overview$n_flagged)` of `r sum(performance$overview$nrep)` fits.
A few flags among many clean fits are expected from a finite sampler.
Flags concentrated at one household count call for more `steps` at that size.

## At the observed size

Each credible interval against the value that generated its study, at the `r n_houses` households of Frederick:

```{r}
#| label: interval-plot
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Three panels, one per parameter. Each shows credible intervals,
#|  one per replicate, around a horizontal line at the true value.
#|  Intervals that miss the line are drawn in orange.
library(ggplot2)

performance$estimates |>
  dplyr::filter(houses == n_houses) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rep, y = estimate)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = cri_lower, ymax = cri_upper, colour = covers)) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = truth)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "black", `FALSE` = "coral"),
                      labels = c(`TRUE` = "covered", `FALSE` = "missed")) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "replicate", y = "estimate", colour = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: observed-size
#| include: false
observed <- subset(performance$summarise(), houses == n_houses)
rownames(observed) <- observed$variable
```

A reasonable performance check shows intervals scattered around the target line, whereas intervals stacked on one side of it would be bias.
An interval that misses the truth on a flagged fit points at the sampler rather than at the model.
At this size the 95% intervals cover the truth in `r round(100 * observed["alpha", "coverage"])`% of the replicates for `alpha`, `r round(100 * observed["beta", "coverage"])`% for `beta`, and `r round(100 * observed["gamma", "coverage"])`% for `gamma`.
`$summarise()` reports each measure next to its Monte Carlo standard error [@morris_using_2019].
Over `r observed["alpha", "nrep"]` replicates, a coverage of 95% is known only to about ±`r round(100 * sqrt(0.95 * 0.05 / observed["alpha", "nrep"]))` percentage points, so a coverage a few points below 95% is no evidence of intervals too narrow.

## Bias across sizes

The error of every estimate relative to the truth, at each household count, is distributed as follows:

```{r}
#| label: bias-plot
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Three panels, one per parameter, on a shared vertical axis. Each shows
#|  one box per household count over the relative error of the estimates, against a line at zero.
performance$estimates |>
  dplyr::mutate(rel_error = estimate / truth - 1) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(houses), y = rel_error)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable) +
  labs(x = "number of households", y = "relative error")
```

Each box spans the middle half of the estimates, so it shows how far a single study of that size lands from the truth.
A box that narrows as households are added is a study buying precision, and one that stays off zero while it narrows is an estimator centered on the wrong value.

## What a larger study buys

A larger study costs more to collect, and more to fit.
We put the width of the credible interval on each parameter next to the seconds it takes to draw 1000 effective samples.
A fit is only as usable as its worst-mixing parameter, so the effective sample size (ESS) is here the smallest bulk ESS over the parameters [@vehtari_rank_normalization_2021]:

```{r}
#| label: design-table
n_vars <- length(names(performance$truth))

cost <- performance$overview |>
  dplyr::summarise(cost = 1000 * secs_per_ess, .by = "houses")

performance$summarise() |>
  dplyr::select(houses, variable, cri_width) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = cri_width) |>
  dplyr::left_join(cost, by = "houses") |>
  flextable::flextable() |>
  flextable::colformat_double(digits = 3) |>
  flextable::colformat_double(j = "cost", digits = 1) |>
  flextable::add_header_row(values = c("houses", "CrI width", "cost"),
                            colwidths = c(1, n_vars, 1)) |>
  flextable::merge_v(part = "header") |>
  flextable::labelizor(labels = c(houses = "n. households",
                                  cost = "seconds per 1000 ESS")) |>
  flextable::align(align = "center", part = "all") |>
  flextable::autofit()
```

```{r}
#| label: doubling
#| include: false
width <- performance$summarise()[c("houses", "variable", "cri_width")] |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = houses, values_from = cri_width)
narrower <- 1 - width[[as.character(2 * n_houses)]] /
  width[[as.character(n_houses)]]
secs <- setNames(cost$cost, cost$houses)
slower <- secs[[as.character(2 * n_houses)]] /
  secs[[as.character(n_houses)]] - 1
```

Doubling the sample size narrows the intervals by `r round(100 * min(narrower))`% to `r round(100 * max(narrower))`%, but makes 1000 effective draws `r round(100 * slower)`% slower to collect.
